n1.text: In {park}, King Kenny stands beneath the old oak, looking up. His red kite is wedged in the highest branches, tail fluttering. "It was only a small gust," he says. "Any ideas? I'd rather not climb."

n2.text: In {jackWorkshop}, Jack listens, wipes his hands on his apron and nods. "Kites in trees are a classic. Two options: a long hooked pole, or my ladder with someone steady holding it."

choices.label: Ask Jack to bring the ladder

n3.text: Robin leans out of {jokerCaravan} with a grin. "A stuck kite! Solve my riddle first: what goes up, but needs a string to come back down?" A top hat on the table seems to be listening.

choices.label: Ask for a real trick instead

n4.text: Queen Rose pours tea in {queenParlour}. "Never rush a kite," she says. "Either borrow something long and sensible from {bakery}, or sit with a cup and let the breeze change its mind."

n5.text: Back in {park}, Jack hooks the pole through the kite's string and lifts it, slow as threading a needle. The kite slips free and floats down into King Kenny's hands. "Splendid," he says. "Tea is on me."

n6.text: You hold the ladder steady while Jack climbs three careful rungs and reaches. The kite comes free. King Kenny applauds as though it were a performance. Jack bows, a little pink, and folds the ladder away.

n7.text: "A kite!" Robin cries, delighted, though you only guessed. From the top hat comes a long chain of knotted scarves with a small beanbag on one end. "Toss it over the branch. Magic is mostly knots."

choices.label: Take the scarves to the Park

n8.text: Robin arrives at {park} and flourishes a cape. "Watch closely. Nothing in my hands, nothing up my sleeves." A breeze lifts, the kite slides off its branch and drifts down. Robin looks quite as surprised as everyone else, then bows anyway.

n9.text: After a second cup, you and Queen Rose stroll to {park}. The wind has turned. As you reach the oak, the kite slips from the branches and settles on a bench. "Patience," says Queen Rose, "is a form of cleverness."

n10.text: The beanbag arcs over the branch on your second try and drops neatly. Together you ease the kite loose with the scarves. King Kenny wears the longest one as a cape all afternoon, and Robin does not ask for it back.

n11.text: At {bakery}, the baker wipes flour from her hands and hands over a long wooden peel, the sort used for reaching the back of the oven. "Bring it back warm," she says, "or with a loaf's worth of thanks."

choices.label: Take the peel to the Park

n12.text: King Kenny holds the oak steady, laughing, while you nudge the kite with the peel. It tumbles down in a flurry of red. Later you return the peel with a bag of sweet buns, bought from the baker with the King's coins.
